description:
Every human body gives off a faint visible light, produced by ordinary cell activity rather than the bioluminescence seen in jellyfish or fireflies. In 2009, Japanese researchers proved it by sealing volunteers in a completely dark room and photographing them with a camera sensitive enough to detect single photons.

roughly how many times too faint for the naked eye this light is. It is real, measurable light, just far below what human vision can register.

The glow is not constant. It follows a daily rhythm, dimmest in the morning and brightest in the late afternoon, and the face gives off more of it than other areas measured. Nobody feels any of this happening. It only shows up on camera.

led the Tohoku Institute of Technology team that produced the first clear images of this light, published in the journal PLOS ONE.

The likely source is free radicals, reactive by-products of normal metabolism, colliding with fats and proteins in skin cells and releasing a tiny burst of light energy each time.

Sources:
- https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0006256: Kobayashi et al.'s 2009 PLOS ONE paper, imaging ultraweak spontaneous photon emission from the human body and confirming that it follows a diurnal rhythm, rising and falling in intensity across the day and peaking in the late afternoon, with the face producing more light than other areas measured.
- https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/photographing-the-glow-of-the-human-body: reports that the study used an ultra-sensitive camera capable of detecting single photons to photograph volunteers in complete darkness, that the light the human body gives off is roughly 1,000 times too faint for the naked eye to detect, and that researchers link the glow to free radicals produced by ordinary cell metabolism reacting with fats and proteins.
